issues.legal_issue: A building that is reasonably suitable or adaptable for residential use is residential accommodation even when it was let for commercial use.
material_facts: The landlord had let the building to a company for business use and for the residence of its manager.
The building had been constructed on land granted for residential construction, remained in residential use in part, and was suitable for residential use.
The landlord sought possession after being directed to vacate government residential accommodation because he owned the building.
issues.conclusion: The building qualified as residential accommodation for the purpose of the landlord’s claim, notwithstanding that it had also been let for commercial use.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(i), premises may be residential, commercial or for another use. For section 14A, residential character is determined by suitability or adaptability for residential use in the context and purpose of the legislation; the purpose of the lease is not conclusive. The contrast with section 14(1)(e), which expressly refers to premises let for residential purposes, supports that interpretation. The Court relied on the legislative purpose described in Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and cited Gillespie Brothers & Co. Ltd. v. Roy Bowles Transport Ltd. and Anderson v. Abbott in support of a contextual rather than absurdly literal construction.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks expedited recovery of a let property after being required to leave government-provided residential accommodation because the landlord owns residential accommodation.
predicates.property_reasonably_suitable_for_residen: The property can reasonably accommodate residential use, either as built or after adaptation.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings this kind of expedited eviction proceeding, a property reasonably suitable for residential use qualifies as residential accommodation.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant must be granted leave to contest an expedited eviction application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would defeat the landlord’s claim to possession.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest the landlord’s expedited eviction application.
The tenant argued that the building’s mixed commercial and residential use meant the landlord could not rely on the special recovery ground.
The Court held that the building’s character did not defeat the landlord’s claim and that the affidavit disclosed no facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovering possession.
issues.conclusion: The Controller was justified in refusing leave to contest because the tenant’s affidavit did not disclose facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25B(5) requires leave where the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession. Disclosure of such facts is a sine qua non for leave. The provision is not to be equated with Order 37, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure: its social setting, subject matter and deliberately narrower language limit the scope for permitting a defence.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks expedited eviction under a special procedure that requires the tenant to obtain leave to contest.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_defeati: The tenant’s affidavit states facts which, if established, would prevent the landlord from obtaining possession on the asserted ground.

issues.definition: In a special expedited eviction proceeding, leave to contest must be granted when the tenant’s affidavit states facts that would defeat the possession claim.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking expedited possession after being required to leave government-provided accommodation must seek the property for the landlord’s own occupation.
material_facts: The landlord was required to vacate government-provided residential accommodation because he owned a building that had been let to a tenant.
The landlord applied for immediate possession of that building under the special recovery procedure.
The Court understood the scheme as addressing the landlord’s consequent need to recover and occupy the landlord’s own property.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s application may be entertained only on the representation that, having been required to vacate the government accommodation, the landlord requires possession of the owned property for personal occupation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read section 14A together with the connected provisions, including the non obstante clause and the summary procedure in section 25B, and treated the own-occupation requirement reflected in section 19 as applying mutatis mutandis. The statutory scheme creates an immediate recovery right to meet the landlord’s need to occupy the landlord’s own residence, not merely the fact of a government order to vacate.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks immediate recovery of a let property through an expedited eviction procedure.
predicates.landlord_required_to_leave_government_re: The landlord has been required to leave residential accommodation provided by the government or a public authority.
predicates.landlord_represents_need_for_personal_oc: The landlord states that possession of the owned property is required for the landlord’s own occupation.

issues.definition: In this kind of expedited proceeding, a landlord required to leave government-provided housing must represent that the owned property is needed for personal occupation.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord who obtains expedited possession but relets the property or fails to occupy it without reasonable cause abuses the judicial process and may have the eviction order cancelled and possession restored to the tenant.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the landlord could obtain possession through the expedited procedure and then relet the property for higher rent rather than occupy it.

The Court held that the statutory scheme requires the landlord’s claim to be for personal occupation and that a later re-letting or failure to occupy without reasonable cause would amount to abuse of process.
issues.conclusion: If possession is obtained and the landlord relets the property or fails to occupy it without reasonable cause, the eviction order may be cancelled and possession restored to the tenant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a court or tribunal must prevent its process from being misused and must give effect to the real purpose of the statutory scheme. It invoked the maxims actus curiae neminem gravabit and actus legis nemini facit injuriam, and relied on the reasoning concerning unconscionable use of legal rights in Gillespie Brothers & Co. Ltd. v. Roy Bowles Transport Ltd., Anderson v. Abbott, and the discussion of D’Cench Duhme. The Court also referred to the inherent power of the judicial process to prevent its machinery from being made a sham.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord obtains possession through an expedited eviction procedure based on a claimed need to occupy the property.
predicates.possession_obtained_for_personal_occupat: The landlord has obtained possession after representing that it is needed for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.property_relet_to_another: After obtaining possession, the landlord lets the property to another person instead of occupying it.
predicates.landlord_fails_to_occupy_without_reasona: After obtaining possession, the landlord does not occupy the property and has no reasonable cause for that failure.

issues.definition: When possession obtained for personal occupation is followed by re-letting or unjustified non-occupation, the eviction order may be cancelled and possession restored.

issues.legal_issue: A government determination that an officer’s property is residential accommodation is relevant but does not foreclose judicial review.
material_facts: The landlord was directed to vacate government-provided residential accommodation on the ground that he owned residential accommodation.
The tenant disputed whether the let building was residential accommodation.
The Court said that a court may ultimately examine the validity of the government’s determination, while ordinarily giving it due weight.
issues.conclusion: The government’s determination should ordinarily be treated as correct, but it is not conclusive and may be invalidated for perversity or mala fides.
issues.legal_principle: The judicial process retains the final power to decide whether the property is residential accommodation. A court should respect, but is not bound by, the administrative determination; perversity or mala fides can invalidate it.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks expedited recovery after a government authority has required the landlord to vacate public residential accommodation on the basis of owned residential property.
predicates.government_determines_property_is_reside: The government authority treats the landlord’s owned property as residential accommodation when directing the landlord to vacate public housing.

issues.definition: In this kind of proceeding, a government determination that the owned property is residential receives due weight but does not bind the court conclusively.
